newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban battle in conquered city, cross key pass.
newsitem.headline: Taleban battle in conquered city, cross key pass.

text.p: The Taleban Islamic militia fought pitched battles against Shi'ite Moslems in this newly conquered northern Afghan city on Tuesday, as other Taleban forces reported crossing a key pass into opposition areas.
Heavy fighting raged for hours in Mazar-i-Sharif after armed Shi'ite residents killed three looters said to belong to the purist Taleban militia.

The Taleban government said its forces had crossed the strategic Salang Pass north of the capital Kabul and marched deep into former opposition territory after being blocked for two days by shelling and a damaged road.

A Taleban spokesman, quoted by a private Afghan news service based in neighbouring Pakistan, said Taleban's supreme leader Mullah Mohammad Omar had accepted an offer of peace talks from opposition guerrilla commander Ahmad Shah Masood.

The Afghan Islamic Press quoted spokesman Abdul Wakil as saying that Omar had told Defence Minister Mullah Obaidullah to talk to Masood, the top military commander of ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani, via radio.

The United Arab Emirates on Tuesday became the third country, after Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, to accord formal diplomatic recognition to the Taleban government, which was was set up after the militia, led by Islamic theology students, captured Kabul last September and which controls nearly 90 percent of the war-shattered country.

Machinegun fire rattled through the streets of Mazar-i-Sharif amid the crash of rocket-propelled grenades and other heavy weapons as the Taleban battled the Shi'ite ethnic Hazaras in the city's northern district of Saidabad.

It was not immediately clear if troops led by ethnic Uzbek General Abdul Malik, who allied with the Taleban last week after staging a mutiny against opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, were involved in the clashes that spread across many parts of the city by late afternoon.

Malik's men, who had forced Dostum to flee Afghanistan on Saturday, were supposed to be operating jointly with the Taleban in the north. It was not immediately clear whether the Uzbeks were fighting the Shi'ites.
Some residents said soldiers under the command of Malik's half-brother, General Gul Mohammad Pahlwan, had joined the Shi'ites against the Taleban, but this could not be confirmed.
The fighting started at about 5.30 p.m. (1300 gmt) and eased after around 9 p.m. (1630 gmt), but bursts of gunfire and explosions could still be heard late into the night.
The Taleban moved into the mainly Hazara tribe district of Mazar-i-Sharif to disarm local people seen as supporters of the anti-Taleban Hezb-i-Wahadat militia force.

On Tuesday morning, Shi'ite residents shot at least three Taleban fighters they said had been caught looting, in the most serious incident since the Taleban arrived in Mazar-i-Sharif on Sunday, a day after Malik captured the city.
One witness said one of Malik's generals dissuaded Taleban forces from entering Saidabad soon after the killings. But shooting and explosions erupted a few hours later.
"All the people started fighting the Taleban because they were taking television sets and everything from people's homes, even children's toys," said Sadiqullah, a Shi'ite resident.
"They are not human. If they were human we would join them, but they are wild men," he said, quivering with rage.

The Taleban government in Kabul said in a radio broadcast its forces had crossed the strategic 11,000-foot (3,350-metre) high Salang Pass on Tuesday and taken the district of Khenjan in Baghlan province.
The advance, after two days of fighting, will cut the last link between Hezb-i-Wahadat, which is still fighting the Taleban in the central province of Bamiyan, and Masood.
Russia convened a meeting in Moscow on Tuesday with diplomats from the former Soviet states bordering Afghanistan.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Gennady Tarasov told reporters Moscow saw the Taleban advance as an internal Afghan matter but if the borders were violated then measures would be taken under the Collective Security Treaty, under which Russian troops could intervene.
